n: Job reflects on the human condition: every person born of a woman lives only a short time, and that life is full of trouble. These words are often read at funerals.

f.g: A Hebrew way of saying “every mortal human.”

f.w: of few days, and full of trouble

n: We bloom like a flower and are cut down; we pass like a shadow and don’t last.

f.w: He cometh forth like a flower, and is cut down
he fleeth also as a shadow

n: And yet you fix your eyes on such a frail creature and drag me into court with you? Job wonders why God would scrutinize something so small.

f.w: open thine eyes upon such an one
f.g: Pay such close attention to so frail a being.

n: Who can bring something pure out of something impure? No one. Human beings cannot make themselves clean — only God can. Latter-day Saints see this need answered in the Atonement of Jesus Christ.

f.w: Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean?

n: God has already set the length of each life — the number of months and the limits no one can pass.
So look away and let him rest, Job pleads, until he finishes his day like a hired worker.
Job contrasts people with trees. A tree that is cut down still has hope — it can sprout again and grow new shoots.

f.w: there is hope of a tree

n: Even if its roots grow old and its stump dies in the ground...
...at the mere scent of water it buds and puts out branches like a young plant.

f.w: through the scent of water it will bud
f.g: A beautiful image: just a hint of water revives it.

n: But a man dies and lies still; he breathes his last — and where is he? Job asks the oldest human question.
Like water vanishing from a lake or a river drying up...

...so a man lies down and doesn’t rise, not until the heavens are gone. Job’s words leave a door open: “till the heavens be no more.” Scripture later teaches that the dead will indeed awake at the resurrection.

f.w: till the heavens be no more
nor be raised out of their sleep

n: Job’s hope begins to rise: if only God would hide him in the grave until His anger passed, then set a time to remember him and bring him back!

f.g: Hebrew Sheol — the world of the dead.

n: The great question: “If a man die, shall he live again?” Job resolves to wait through his hard service until his “change” comes. Later he will testify, “I know that my redeemer liveth” (Job 19:25). Latter-day Saints affirm the answer through Christ’s resurrection.

f.w: If a man die, shall he live again?

f.g: Relief, release — like a soldier relieved at the end of his duty.

n: You will call, and I will answer; you will long for the creature your hands have made. Job glimpses a loving God who yearns for His children.

f.w: thou wilt have a desire to the work of thine hands

n: For now, though, God seems to count Job’s every step and keep watch over his sin.
Some read this as hope: God seals Job’s sins in a bag and covers them up — out of sight, as if forgiven. Others read it as God storing up evidence.

f.g: Possibly an image of sins put away and covered — forgiven (compare Micah 7:19).

n: But then Job’s hope fades again. Even mountains crumble and rocks shift from their places.
As water wears away stones and floods wash away soil, so God wears down human hope.

f.g: Slow erosion — a picture of gradual loss.

n: God overpowers a person forever; He changes his face in death and sends him away.
The dead don’t know whether their children rise to honor or fall into disgrace. Job, who lost all his children, feels this keenly.
He feels only his own pain and mourns only for himself. The chapter ends in sorrow — yet the question of verse 14 has been raised, and the book will return to it.

f.w: his soul within him shall mourn
